Happy Copadichromis likomae is a maternal mouthbrooding cichlid endemic to Lake Malawi, where it inhabits the intermediate rocky-sedimentary zones along the eastern coast. Adults in this population reach a maximum body length of 14 centimeters [Li = 14 centimeters], a size that aligns well with the typical dimensions reported for congeners within the Copadichromis genus. Field surveys indicate that the onset of gonadal activity and the transition to a reproductively competent state occur when individuals attain a total body length of 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters], which corresponds to the size at which puberty is first documented in wild-caught specimens. The mass of newly emerged larvae, measured immediately after the yolk-sac larva emerges from the egg, is approximately 0.023 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.023 grams], a modest starting weight that reflects the limited yolk reserves available for endotrophic development prior to the onset of exogenous feeding. This neonatal mass is comparable to values estimated for related species in the genus, such as Copadichromis chrysonotus, from which morphological data on egg size have been extrapolated.

The relationship between body size and mass in Happy follows a power-law function derived from a broader dataset on cichlid morphometrics, and this allometric scaling allows estimation of mass at key developmental milestones. At the total length of 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters] associated with sexual maturation, the predicted wet weight is approximately 10.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 10.3 grams], indicating that fish at the onset of puberty already possess a substantial somatic mass relative to their ultimate adult size. The maximum adult wet weight, corresponding to the asymptote of the length-weight relationship at the ultimate total length of 14 centimeters [Li = 14 centimeters], is 38.4 grams [Wwi = 38.4 grams]. This adult mass is attained gradually over the species' growth trajectory, with individuals investing considerable time in somatic development before allocating resources toward reproductive effort. The consistency of these scaling relationships across related species suggests a conserved body plan among the utaka cichlids, although local ecological conditions in Lake Malawi may introduce minor variation in the length-weight parameters.

Reproductive output in Happy has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], which approximates the thermal regime experienced by the species during the cooler months of the year in its native habitat. Under these conditions, gravid individuals produce clutches averaging 50 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 50 eggs per spawning event], and the available evidence indicates that females undertake a single spawning event annually [F_R_i = single spawning event annually]. This reproductive strategy, combining a moderate clutch size with a low annual frequency, is typical of many maternal mouthbrooding cichlids, which invest heavily in parental care by carrying the developing eggs and larvae in the buccal cavity. The temperature regime is notably cooler than the peak summer temperatures of the lake, and it is likely that reproductive timing in the wild is influenced by seasonal thermal cycles that promote spawning during periods of optimal food availability for the ensuing larval stages.

Longevity data for Happy, also collected from individuals maintained at 19 °C [T = 19 °C], reveal that the maximum documented lifespan in captivity is 6 years [am = 6 years], a relatively long duration for a cichlid of this body size and one that reflects the species' measured life-history pace. This lifespan, equivalent to approximately 2190 days, is consistent with the slow growth and delayed reproduction observed in the species, traits that are often associated with stable environments where adult survival is favored over high fecundity. In comparison to other Lake Malawi cichlids, the maximum recorded longevity of 6 years [am = 6 years] places Happy in an intermediate position, shorter than that of some large predatory species but considerably longer than that of small, short-lived haplochromines at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. The thermal conditions at which these observations were made are critical, as metabolic rate and senescence are both temperature-dependent processes, and the value of 6 years [am = 6 years] may shift under the warmer temperatures typical of the lake's surface waters during the austral summer at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C].

The interplay between size at puberty, adult body mass, and reproductive output in Happy provides insight into its ecological role as a zooplanktivore within the pelagic zone of Lake Malawi. The substantial difference between the wet weight at puberty of approximately 10.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 10.3 grams] and the ultimate wet weight of 38.4 grams [Wwi = 38.4 grams] indicates that individuals more than triple their body mass between the attainment of sexual maturity and the approach of their maximum size, a pattern that suggests continued somatic growth well after reproductive activation has begun. This growth trajectory, coupled with a modest annual reproductive rate and an extended lifespan of 6 years [am = 6 years], aligns with the characteristics of an equilibrium life-history strategy, which is commonly observed in species that experience relatively stable but resource-limited environments at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. The total length at puberty of 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters] and the neonatal mass of approximately 0.023 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.023 grams] further underscore the species' investment in producing relatively large, well-provisioned offspring that can begin exogenous feeding with a size advantage over smaller competitors.
